package_info.why_malicious: Vulnerable versions of the CUPS printing stack, when configured with default settings, allow remote attackers to achieve arbitrary code execution by exploiting a chain of vulnerabilities. Attackers can remotely install a malicious printer via UDP port 631, deliver a crafted PPD file containing a FoomaticRIPCommandLine directive with arbitrary shell commands, and trigger code execution when a print job is processed. This enables remote code execution without authentication, compromising system integrity.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker sends a UDP packet to port 631 containing a URL to an attacker-controlled IPP server.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon receiving a UDP packet to port 631, the cups-browsed service parses the packet, extracts the reference to a remote IPP server, and initiates a connection to the attacker's server, enabling remote printer installation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accepting remote printer definitions via unauthenticated UDP packets from untrusted sources exposes the system to remote manipulation and unauthorized device addition.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Printer discovery should be limited to trusted local networks or authenticated sources, not arbitrary remote hosts on the internet.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate printer discovery within a trusted local network using mDNS or SLP.
key_indicators: UDP port 631 exposed to external or untrusted networks
cups-browsed service accepting printer definitions from unauthenticated sources
Unexpected remote printer URLs in network traffic

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: CUPS makes a POST request to the attacker-controlled IPP server to fetch printer attributes (Get-Printer-Attributes).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After receiving the printer reference, CUPS initiates an outbound HTTP/IPP connection to the attacker's server, sends a Get-Printer-Attributes request, receives a crafted set of printer attributes including a malicious PPD file, and prepares to install the printer with attacker-supplied configuration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching printer configuration and PPD files from an untrusted remote server allows the attacker to supply arbitrary and potentially malicious configuration data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Printer attribute retrieval should be restricted to trusted, authenticated network printers, not arbitrary external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Fetching printer attributes from known, trusted network printers within an enterprise environment.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP/IPP requests to unknown or external IPP servers
Unvalidated or unauthenticated printer attribute data received
PPD files sourced from remote, non-whitelisted servers

execution_context.trigger: file creation (PPD file written to disk)
execution_context.file_location: Temporary directory for PPD files (e.g., /tmp/ or /var/spool/cups/tmp/)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: CUPS writes a PPD file containing a FoomaticRIPCommandLine directive with attacker-supplied shell commands.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the PPD file is written to disk, it contains a FoomaticRIPCommandLine directive embedding arbitrary shell commands provided by the attacker, staging these commands for execution during subsequent print jobs.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Allowing arbitrary shell commands in PPD files from untrusted sources enables attackers to inject code that will be executed by the printing subsystem.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: PPD files should only contain trusted configuration data and should not allow untrusted or arbitrary command execution directives.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom PPDs for advanced printer features, but only when sourced from trusted administrators or vendors.
key_indicators: FoomaticRIPCommandLine directive with shell metacharacters in PPD files
PPD files written to /tmp/ or /var/spool/cups/tmp/ from remote sources
Presence of suspicious or non-standard shell commands in PPD content

execution_context.trigger: user action (print job sent to malicious printer)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: foomatic-rip executes the shell command specified in the FoomaticRIPCommandLine directive from the malicious PPD file.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When a print job is sent to the malicious printer, the foomatic-rip process is invoked, reads the FoomaticRIPCommandLine directive from the PPD file, executes the embedded shell command, and results in arbitrary code execution under the privileges of the printing service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Execution of attacker-supplied shell commands as a result of a print job is a direct code execution vulnerability, enabling full system compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Print jobs should not trigger execution of arbitrary shell commands from untrusted PPD files; only trusted, administrator-approved filters should be executed.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom print filters or scripts for advanced printing features, but only when managed by trusted administrators.
key_indicators: foomatic-rip process spawning unexpected child processes
Shell commands executed from PPD file content
Print job logs showing execution of non-standard or suspicious commands

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a UDP packet to port 631 with a reference to a malicious IPP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim CUPS service initiates connection to attacker's IPP server.

attack_chain.action: CUPS fetches printer attributes and a malicious PPD file from the attacker's IPP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious PPD file is written to disk.

attack_chain.action: CUPS writes the attacker-supplied PPD file containing a FoomaticRIPCommandLine directive.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious command is staged for execution.

attack_chain.action: User triggers a print job to the malicious printer, causing foomatic-rip to execute the attacker's command.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution on the victim system (final goal).

behavioral_signatures: Inbound UDP packets to port 631 from untrusted or external sources
CUPS making outbound HTTP/IPP connections to unknown or non-whitelisted IPP servers
Creation of PPD files containing FoomaticRIPCommandLine directives with shell metacharacters or suspicious commands
foomatic-rip process spawning unexpected child processes or executing non-standard shell commands
file_indicators: PPD files in /tmp/, /var/spool/cups/tmp/, or similar directories containing FoomaticRIPCommandLine directives with shell commands
foomatic-rip process execution logs showing invocation of shell commands from PPD files
Presence of PPD files sourced from remote, unauthenticated servers
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/IPP requests from CUPS to suspicious or external IP addresses or domains
Inbound UDP traffic to port 631 from the internet or non-local networks
Unexpected remote printer URLs in network traffic logs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for inbound UDP traffic to port 631, especially from untrusted or external sources. Alert on CUPS making outbound HTTP/IPP connections to unknown or non-whitelisted IPP servers. Scan newly created PPD files for FoomaticRIPCommandLine directives containing shell metacharacters or suspicious commands. Monitor foomatic-rip process executions and flag any unexpected child processes or command-line arguments. Correlate these events to identify the full attack chain and distinguish malicious activity from legitimate printer discovery and configuration.
